## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Uddhata Sutta* (Ud 4.2, PTS Ud 37) is the second discourse of the fourth chapter (*Meghiya Vagga*) of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral]. The sutta focuses on the spiritual necessity of protecting both body and mind [SuttaCentral]. While modern secondary literature in the dossier does not provide a dedicated study of this specific discourse, its stock descriptive formula characterizing agitated and undisciplined monks (*uddhatā unnaḷā capalā...*) appears widely in canonical contexts, and Mrs. Rhys Davids cites the Udāna commentary (UdA 238) for its traditional glosses on these behavioral terms [Mrs. Rhys Davids 1929].
The verse portion of the sutta corresponds closely to the "Mind" chapter found in various recensions of the northern verse collections. Curated parallels identified on SuttaCentral include the *Cittavarga* of the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UV 31), its Tibetan translation (*Uv Kg* 31), and two Chinese recensions preserved in the Taishō Canon (T 212.32 and T 213.31) [SuttaCentral]. Machine alignments from DharmaNexus confirm these relationships with high plausibility scores, showing extensive verse correspondence between segments §3.1–4.2 and the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* as well as two Tibetan recensions (D4099 and D0326) [DharmaNexus].
Within the Pali textual tradition, SuttaCentral records citations of the discourse across multiple hermeneutical sections of the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 10, Ne 20, Ne 22, and Ne 35) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches support this usage, identifying text reuse of verse segments §4.4–5.6 in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Nettivibhāvinī* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus records substantial narrative prose reuse (§0.2–2.1) shared with the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51.14), along with shorter phrase parallels in the *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6.61) and the *Yakkha Saṁyutta* (SN 10.3) [DharmaNexus].
